track.name: prompt-eng
track.label: Prompt Engineering & AI Tools
track.summary: Master the art and science of writing effective prompts for ChatGPT, Claude, and AI coding tools. Learn proven patterns, automate workflows, and use AI responsibly at work.

phases.title: Foundations of Prompting
phases.description: Build a solid mental model of how language models respond to instructions. Cover zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, and the role of system prompts.

phases.title: ChatGPT & Claude for Work
phases.description: Apply prompting to real workplace tasks: summarising documents, drafting content, extracting structured data, and classifying text at scale.

phases.title: Cursor & Copilot for Non-Engineers
phases.description: Use AI code editors to write scripts, automate spreadsheets, and debug errors even without a software engineering background.

phases.title: Prompt Patterns & Templates
phases.description: Study reusable prompt architectures: ReAct, Tree of Thought, prompt chaining, and meta-prompts that generate other prompts.

phases.title: AI Workflows & Automation
phases.description: Chain multiple AI tools together, automate repetitive document and data tasks, and bring AI assistants into spreadsheets.

phases.title: Evaluation & Safety
phases.description: Test prompt outputs systematically, detect hallucinations, and apply responsible-use principles for AI at work.

topics.title: Zero-Shot and Few-Shot Prompting
topics.description: Understand the difference between zero-shot and few-shot prompting, and learn when to provide examples to steer model output.

steps.d: Ask a model to classify an email subject line without examples and note the answer.
Rewrite the same prompt with two labelled email examples, then classify the same email again.
Compare the zero-shot and two-shot classifications and document which was more consistent.
Add five carefully chosen examples to the prompt and classify the emails a third time, noting any improvement.
Write a one-sentence note on which email types benefited from examples and where zero-shot worked equally well.

topics.title: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
topics.description: Learn how asking a model to think step-by-step (chain-of-thought) dramatically improves accuracy on complex tasks.

steps.d: Ask a model to solve a multi-step maths problem (e.g. revenue calculation) and note the answer.
Ask the same question with 'Let's think step by step' prepended and capture the answer and reasoning.
Check both answers for correctness and count how many reasoning steps appeared in the second response.
Take a complex question from your work and prompt for step-by-step reasoning instead of a direct answer.
Run your business task twice with and without 'think step by step' and document which response was more usable.

topics.title: Roles, Personas, and System Prompts
topics.description: Craft system-level instructions and assign personas to control tone, expertise level, and response style consistently.

steps.d: Set the system prompt to 'You are a senior product manager with 10 years of experience' and ask it to critique a feature request.
Send the same feature request to the model without the system prompt and compare tone and depth.
Rewrite the system prompt to request a 'skeptical CFO' and ask the same question, noting how the response shifts focus.
Add to the system prompt 'Keep your response to 150 words' and 'Respond only with actionable items', then re-run the critique.
Ask five different follow-up questions about the feature with the same system prompt and verify the persona maintains consistent tone.

topics.title: Summarisation Prompts
topics.description: Build prompts that reliably condense long documents, meeting notes, and articles into actionable summaries.

steps.d: Create a prompt asking the model to summarise a multi-paragraph news article into three bullet points and test on a real article.
Rewrite the prompt to request 'Key event, Impact, and Next steps' as three sections instead of bullets and re-summarise.
Revise the prompt to request 'exactly 50 words' and measure whether the output stays within the limit.
Apply your prompt to three different document types (meeting notes, research paper, email thread) and note any needed rephrasing.
Write your own summary of one document by hand, run your prompt on the same document, and identify what the AI missed or added.

topics.title: Drafting and Editing with AI
topics.description: Use AI to draft emails, reports, and proposals, then iterate with feedback prompts to polish the output.

steps.d: Ask the model to 'Draft a professional follow-up email to a client after a sales call' and copy the output.
Reply with 'Make this less formal and more friendly' and run the prompt again with the same context.
Ask the model to 'shorten this to two paragraphs' or 'expand to four paragraphs' and re-generate the email.
Point out a line you don't like and ask for alternatives to that specific part.
Confirm your edited AI draft is ready by copying it into a real email and setting a send time.

topics.title: Extraction and Classification
topics.description: Pull structured data from unstructured text and classify documents, feedback, or support tickets using well-crafted prompts.

steps.d: Write a prompt to 'Extract name, email, and product interest from this support ticket and return as JSON' and test on five tickets.
Create a classification prompt that sorts customer feedback into 'Positive', 'Negative', or 'Neutral' and test on 10 real entries.
Modify your prompt to end with 'Return only valid JSON' and validate that each response is parseable.
Run your prompt on five edge cases (empty input, multiple products, unclear tone) and refine it to handle them.
Take your best prompt and copy it into a spreadsheet formula or Zapier action to process new data automatically.

topics.title: AI Code Editors Overview
topics.description: Get oriented with Cursor and GitHub Copilot — how they work, when to use each, and how to configure them for your workflow.

steps.d: Download and install Cursor or enable GitHub Copilot in your IDE, then open a blank Python or JavaScript file.
Type a comment like '# Function to parse CSV file' and press Tab or Ctrl+Enter to see AI-generated code, then accept or reject.
Use inline completion to write a small function, then open the chat panel and describe the same task to compare outputs.
Open the chat panel and describe a small script (e.g. 'Read a CSV file, filter rows where age > 30, write to a new file'), then review the code.
Copy the generated code into a file, save it, and run it on real data to verify it works as intended.

topics.title: Writing Scripts with AI Assistance
topics.description: Use AI suggestions to write Python or JavaScript scripts for data processing, file manipulation, and API calls without prior coding experience.

steps.d: Open the chat and describe: 'I have a CSV with customer names and purchase dates; find the customer with the most recent purchase.'
Copy the generated script into a file, read through it line by line, and personalise it by changing one variable name or function call.
Save the script and execute it with your own CSV file to verify the output is correct.
Go back to the chat and ask: 'Modify this to find customers with purchases in the last 30 days' and apply the changes.
Save your script and set up scheduling (Windows Task Scheduler or cron) to run it on a regular interval.

topics.title: Debugging and Code Review with AI
topics.description: Describe error messages to AI, receive plain-English explanations, and apply suggested fixes confidently.

steps.d: Copy a full error message from your console and ask the AI: 'What does this error mean and how do I fix it?'
Review the AI's explanation and ask for clarification on any terms you don't understand in simpler words.
Follow the AI's suggested fix (e.g. update a function call, add a missing import, change a loop condition) in your code.
Run your script again to verify the error is gone and the code produces the expected output.
Write a one-sentence note about what caused the error and how you fixed it for future reference.

topics.title: ReAct and Structured Reasoning Patterns
topics.description: Apply the ReAct pattern (Reason + Act) to build prompts that interleave thinking and action steps for complex problems.

steps.d: Create a prompt with the structure: 'Thought: [reasoning], Action: [what to do], Observation: [result]' and test on a planning task.
Ask the model to 'Use Thought/Action/Observation format to answer: What are the top three industries for AI investment in 2026?'
Copy the response and mark each Thought, Action, and Observation with brackets to see how many cycles the model ran.
Rewrite the prompt to add constraints like 'Do not repeat the same observation twice' or 'Stop after 4 rounds', then re-run.
Run the same question once with ReAct format and once without, then compare the depth and accuracy of both responses.

topics.title: Tree of Thought and Prompt Chaining
topics.description: Explore Tree of Thought for multi-path reasoning and learn how to chain prompts so the output of one feeds the next.

steps.d: Ask the model to 'Use Tree of Thought to explore three different ways to structure a weekly meeting agenda' and review the branches explored.
Write Prompt 1 to 'Outline five blog post ideas on AI prompt engineering', then write Prompt 2 to 'Expand the third idea into a one-paragraph summary' using Prompt 1's output.
Copy the exact output from Prompt 1 into Prompt 2 and verify that Prompt 2 correctly references and expands the idea.
Write Prompt 1 → Prompt 2 → Prompt 3 where each builds on the previous output for a real task like writing a product launch plan.
Produce the same output with a single prompt and with your three-prompt chain, then note which was clearer or more useful.

topics.title: Meta-Prompts and Template Libraries
topics.description: Write prompts that generate other prompts, build reusable template libraries, and use AI to iteratively improve your own prompts.

steps.d: Create a meta-prompt like 'Take this prompt and rewrite it to be more specific and include at least one example', then apply it to a weak prompt.
Document 5-10 prompts you use regularly in a file with titles like 'Summarise [topic]', 'Extract data from [format]', 'Draft [document type]'.
Feed each template into your meta-prompt and rewrite any that are vague or missing detail.
Take three of your templates and apply each to a different task (different topic, format, or document type) and note whether tweaking was needed.
Pick your best template, document what it does and how to adapt it, and have a colleague test it on a real task.

topics.title: Combining Multiple AI Tools
topics.description: Design workflows that hand off outputs between ChatGPT, Claude, Zapier, and other AI services to accomplish multi-step tasks.

steps.d: Identify a task that currently requires multiple tools and draw out the steps from start to finish including all tool handoffs.
Sign up for Zapier, connect two apps (such as Gmail and Google Sheets), and test a simple trigger and action.
Configure your Zap to capture output from the first tool (e.g. email subject) and pass it to the second (e.g. add to spreadsheet).
Insert an OpenAI or Claude action in your Zap to process data between the two apps, e.g. summarise the email then add to Sheets.
Trigger your workflow with real data and check that the output lands in the final tool without manual copying.

topics.title: Automating Repetitive Tasks with AI
topics.description: Identify high-volume, low-creativity tasks in your work and set up AI-driven automations that run without your involvement.

steps.d: Write down 3-5 tasks you do weekly that are rule-based and don't require creativity (e.g. moving leads to a folder, tagging tickets, sending reminders).
For each task, estimate minutes per occurrence and weekly frequency, multiply to find total weekly time, then highlight the highest-value targets.
For each high-value task, ask 'Is it repetitive? Is it rule-based? Can I describe the rule clearly?' and mark those with three yeses.
Order your best candidates by potential time saved and difficulty of setup, then pick the easiest one to build first.
Create a Zap or Make scenario that replaces the manual task, using filters or routers to handle edge cases and monitor the first three runs.

topics.title: AI Assistants in Spreadsheets
topics.description: Use Copilot in Excel and AI features in Google Sheets to write formulas, clean data, and generate charts from natural language.

steps.d: Launch Excel or Google Sheets and ensure Microsoft 365 Copilot or Google Sheets AI features are accessible.
Click the Copilot icon and describe a formula you need (e.g. 'Calculate average sale price for orders over $100'), then review the result.
Copy the generated formula into a cell, press Enter, and spot-check that it calculates correctly on your data.
Select your data and ask Copilot to 'Create a line chart showing sales by month' and review the generated chart.
Describe a data task to Copilot (e.g. 'Remove duplicate rows' or 'Split names into first and last columns') and apply the suggested steps.

topics.title: Evaluating and Testing Prompt Outputs
topics.description: Design simple evaluation rubrics and test suites to measure whether your prompts perform reliably across varied inputs.

steps.d: List 3-4 criteria for a task (e.g. for email summaries: 'mentions main topic', 'includes action items', 'under 100 words') and assign a score to each.
Run the same prompt 10 times on different inputs and score each output against your rubric.
Tally how many of the 10 outputs met your criteria fully, partially, or not at all.
Review the 2-3 lowest-scoring outputs and describe what went wrong (e.g. 'missed action items', 'too verbose').
Rewrite the prompt to address the failures (e.g. 'Always include action items in a bulleted list'), then run the same 10 tests again and compare.

topics.title: Hallucination Detection and Grounding
topics.description: Recognise when a model fabricates facts, use grounding techniques to anchor responses in verified sources, and write verification prompts.

steps.d: Take a response about a recent event and ask the model: 'Is everything in that answer verifiable? Point out anything you're uncertain about.'
Use a search engine or trusted source to verify one specific claim from the response and note whether the model fabricated any details.
Create a prompt that asks for an answer followed by 'Cite each claim with a source, or say I don't know' and test on the same question.
Run the original and grounded versions side by side and count how many claims in the grounded version are sourced or qualified.
Create a two-step prompt where the second step asks 'Fact-check your previous response and flag anything you're less than 90% sure about.'

topics.title: Responsible AI Use at Work
topics.description: Understand data-privacy considerations, bias risks, and organisational policies for deploying AI tools in professional settings.

steps.d: Find and review your company's written AI policy covering data privacy and tool approval, or draft one if none exists.
List 3-5 types of data you work with that should not be sent to a public AI tool (e.g. customer records, financial data, source code).
Read the privacy and data-retention policies for your chosen AI tool and document what happens to your inputs.
Write a one-page checklist: 'Before using this tool, I will check: [policy approved it], [no sensitive data], [I can explain the output to my manager].'
Review the last 5-10 prompts you sent to a public AI tool and verify each one complies with your checklist.
